messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Lieutenant Commander Marcus Cole was thirty-four years old, a decorated Navy officer who had served on destroyers and guided-missile cruisers, a man who had always prided himself on his composure under pressure. That composure had been tested three years earlier when his ship, the USS *Vanguard*, was caught in a Category 4 typhoon in the Philippine Sea. He had been the officer of the deck during the worst of it, responsible for the safety of three hundred sailors as the ship rolled forty degrees and waves crashed over the bow. He remembered the screaming of the wind, the shuddering of the hull, the moment a rogue wave smashed a porthole and seawater flooded the berthing compartment, and the hours of scrambling to secure hatches and rescue a young seaman who had been swept against a bulkhead. What stayed with him most, though, was not the chaos but the stillness afterward—the way his hands had trembled uncontrollably for an hour, the way he had stared at his own reflection in a dark window and not recognized the man looking back.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself avoiding things he could not explain. He stopped going to the base gym because it was too crowded; he started taking the long way to his office to avoid the narrow corridor near the mess hall. When his wife suggested a weekend trip to the city, he made excuses about work. He began drinking alone in the evenings, a habit he had never had before, and the smell of alcohol on his own breath would sometimes bring the typhoon rushing back—the metallic tang of seawater, the acrid odor of diesel fuel, the sour sweat of fear. On those nights, he would sit in the dark of his garage, his body rigid, his hands clenched into fists, feeling as though he were still braced against that endless roll. The memory felt so extreme, so impossible, that he sometimes had to remind himself it had really happened. He would replay the images—the flooded berthing, the seaman’s terrified face, the shuddering metal—and each time, he would think, *I should have done more. I deserve this.*

Marcus had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere. At work, his fellow officers seemed distant, their conversations about football and fishing trivial and hollow. He felt isolated, set apart, as if a pane of glass separated him from everyone else. He used to be a happy person, he was certain of that—but now he was always miserable, and he could not remember when that had changed. When a memory surfaced, triggered by a sudden gust of wind or a dark hallway, he would feel his body lock into that same position: feet planted, knees bent, hands gripping an invisible railing. And then the isolation would deepen, because how could anyone understand what it had been like? He told himself he deserved to suffer, and so he stopped answering calls from his old shipmates, stopped accepting invitations to barbecues, stopped walking past the base chapel where he used to sit and think. Each avoidance made the memories feel more unreal, more like a story that had happened to someone else, and the more unreal they felt, the more he felt he had to punish himself for not being able to let it go.

The loop tightened over months. A crowded commissary would send him home early, and at home the darkness of the bedroom would bring back the typhoon, and the typhoon would bring the guilt, and the guilt would drive him to the garage where he would sit in the dark and think, *This is where I belong.* He began to notice that any physical location that reminded him of the ship—a narrow hallway, a room with no windows, a floor that vibrated—would trigger the same bodily reenactment, and then the same spiral of self-blame. He avoided those places, but the avoidance itself became a trigger: every time he took a different route, every time he said no to an invitation, the memory returned, sharper and more punishing. He was certain that if he stopped avoiding, something terrible would happen—that he would fall apart, that his wife would see what he had become, that the Navy would discharge him.

What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a minor thing. His wife had asked him to pick up takeout from a restaurant near the waterfront, and he had driven forty minutes out of his way to avoid the bridge. When he came home, she was crying. She said she did not know who he was anymore. He sat on the edge of the bed, his hands trembling, and he thought about the seaman he had pulled from the flood—how the man had thanked him, how Marcus had said *It’s my job*—and he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt that simple, that clear. He was afraid of what would happen if he stopped punishing himself. He was more afraid of what would happen if he did not.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to memory; the vignette describes memory triggering guilt, but not guilt strengthening the memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to triggers; the vignette does not show guilt or self-blame causing new triggers to appear.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies lead to memory; avoidance is described as triggered by memory, but not as causing or strengthening the memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies lead to triggers; avoidance is described as a response to triggers, not as generating new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In the months that followed, Marcus found himself avoiding things he could not explain. He stopped going to the base gym because it was too crowded; he started taking the long way to his office to avoid the narrow corridor near the mess hall.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The conviction that he deserved to suffer meant that the memory of the flooded berthing compartment surfaced almost daily now, each time more vivid than the last — as if his guilt had sharpened it into a weapon he kept turning over in his hands.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He would replay the images—the flooded berthing, the seaman’s terrified face, the shuddering metal—and each time, he would think, *I should have done more. I deserve this.*
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That same belief — that he deserved what had happened — began to expand the range of things that could trigger him: now even the sound of running water from a faucet or the sight of a puddle on the pavement would snap his attention back to the ship, because his guilt had taught him to see the typhoon everywhere.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Each avoidance made the memories feel more unreal, more like a story that had happened to someone else, and the more unreal they felt, the more he felt he had to punish himself for not being able to let it go.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Not talking about it, never letting himself describe it aloud, meant the memory had never been put into words — it remained in him, undisturbed and intact, exactly where he had left it, waiting to be replayed in full.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He avoided those places, but the avoidance itself became a trigger: every time he took a different route, every time he said no to an invitation, the memory returned, sharper and more punishing.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round he drove to avoid the bridge was its own daily acknowledgement of the typhoon, and the act of rerouting brought the event back into his mind as surely as any direct encounter would have.
<<<END>>>
